lines.text: Last time we traced one write all the way down to a brand new file on disk, never edited again.
Do that forever and you get a problem. Sorted runs just keep piling up, one per flush.
Something has to merge them back down, and that something is compaction. What does it actually cost?
I ran the exact same shuffled write pattern through two of RocksDB's own real compaction styles, measuring the result directly.
Leveled compaction keeps one sorted run per level and merges aggressively. On this workload, it settled down to just three files.
Tiered, which RocksDB itself calls universal compaction, lets more runs coexist before merging. The same writes settled to four files instead.

lines.text: There's a third style that doesn't merge at all.
I wrote well past a configured hundred kilobyte cap on a real FIFO-style store.
The oldest round's own key was simply gone, dropped outright. The newest round's own key was still right there.
So here's the real question these three styles are all dancing around.
Leveled pays more to write. Tiered pays more to read later, because more runs pile up first. Is there a compaction style out there that just avoids all of these costs?
"Somebody just hasn't invented it yet" is a tempting answer. It's also wrong.
This isn't an engineering gap waiting to be closed. It has a name, and a proof sketch behind it.
No compaction style escapes this trade-off, and the next thing I'm going to show you is exactly why.
It's called the RUM conjecture, and it gives each of those costs a precise name.
Read overhead is read amplification. Update overhead is write amplification. Memory overhead is space amplification. Each one is a real ratio, with a theoretical floor of exactly one.
And the conjecture itself says: optimize any two of those three, and the one you didn't touch gets worse. Not usually. Provably.
That trade-off isn't just theory. RocksDB has a real, measured trigger built around it.
I configured the trigger on the newest level, L zero, to two files, then ran a real write pattern and read RocksDB's own internal file count directly.
It came back at six, well past that trigger. At that point RocksDB doesn't crash or block. It deliberately slows writes down, on purpose.

lines.text: Here's the connection.
Last topic, a tombstone was uncollected merge work on a single key, sitting there until some later compaction finally cleaned it up.
A write stall is the exact same debt, just at the scale of the whole system instead of one key, finally forcing a slowdown.

lines.text: This chapter's own lab puts a number on all of this. I ran the identical insert-then-update workload against a real Postgres cluster and a real RocksDB instance, side by side.
Postgres paid roughly two point six one times write amplification and one point eight nine times space amplification. RocksDB paid less on both: about one point eight five and one point one one.

RocksDB's own read came back faster every single run too, but I want to be honest about that one. That's an in-process read against Postgres's own network round trip, not a clean amplification comparison.

lines.text: Pull it together, because none of this was three separate design choices.
Every compaction style you just saw is picking a spot on the exact same read, write and space trade-off, and the conjecture is why none of them can pick a better spot than the others.
The lab didn't just illustrate that idea. It put a real number on what two production engines actually chose to pay for their own spot on it.
One more for you. Picture a workload that's almost all writes, barely ever reads anything back, and disk space costs nothing to it.
The instinct is to reach for the mature, general-purpose default. Is that actually the right call here?
Which engine from this lab genuinely fits that workload: the B-tree, or the LSM tree?

lines.text: "The mature default" is usually a safe bet. Here, it's the wrong one.
This workload cares about exactly one thing: writing cheaply. This chapter's own lab just measured the LSM tree paying less for precisely that.
So it's the LSM tree, not because it's newer, but because the numbers we just measured say so.
